design_notes: 15 topic-matched scenarios, each rewritten once per emotion using only implicit cues (actions, body language, physiology, tone) - no emotion words. Neutral baselines use the same 15 topics with flat, factual phrasing. Neutral filler turns are unrelated topics, fixed and identical across all conditions, used to bridge measurement turns in the persistence/decay experiment.

happy: She hummed along to the radio and grinned at every green light on the way to work.
He walked out of the interview room bouncing on his heels, already picturing his first day.
Everyone burst into laughter around the table, and she couldn't stop smiling through dessert.
The kids pressed their faces to the window, giggling every time thunder rattled the glass.
She read the score twice, let out a whoop, and called her mother immediately.
They danced around the empty living room before a single box was even unpacked.
The whole bench jumped up screaming, arms in the air, as the ball hit the net.
He tasted the sauce, closed his eyes, and did a little spin in the kitchen.
She spotted her sister through the crowd and sprinted the last few steps, laughing the whole way.
The nurse told them the surgery went perfectly, and they hugged each other right there in the hallway.
Balloons bounced off the ceiling as everyone sang off-key, and she couldn't wipe the grin off her face.
He hit send on the final report early, leaned back, and pumped his fist at the screen.
They reached the summit just as the sun broke through, high-fiving and snapping photo after photo.
Her voice jumped an octave the second she recognized who was calling.
The refund landed in her account and she immediately texted three friends with exclamation points.
calm: He rolled the window down halfway and let the quiet drive settle into an easy rhythm.
She sat back in the chair, breathing evenly, answering each question without any rush.
The conversation drifted lazily from topic to topic as plates emptied one by one.
He watched the rain trace lines down the window, wrapped in a blanket with tea in hand.
She glanced at the grade, nodded once, and went back to her book.
They unpacked one box at a time, taking breaks to sit on the porch and watch the street.
He leaned back in his seat, watching the match unfold without checking the score once.
She moved through the recipe slowly, stirring the pot while humming softly to herself.
He found a window seat, put his bag down, and let the gate announcements fade into background noise.
She sat by the bed holding his hand, her breathing slow and steady the whole afternoon.
He drifted between conversations, content to listen more than talk.
She closed her laptop at the usual time, confident the report would be fine either way.
They walked the last mile in silence, matching their pace to the sound of the wind.
His voice stayed even and unhurried as he caught up with the old friend.
She set the envelope on the counter, made a note to deal with it after dinner, and kept reading.
proud: He caught his reflection in the window and straightened his collar, still thinking about yesterday's presentation.
She shook the interviewer's hand firmly, chin up, certain she'd nailed every answer.
Her father raised his glass toward her twice during dinner, grinning the whole time.
He checked the roof he'd repaired himself and watched it hold steady against the wind.
He pinned the certificate to the wall where everyone walking in would see it.
She stood in the doorway of the house she'd saved for years to buy, arms crossed, taking it all in.
He jogged off the field to a row of teammates reaching out to slap his shoulder.
She set the dish down at the center of the table and waited for the first bite, arms folded.
He handed over the boarding pass for the trip he'd planned entirely on his own.
The doctor told her the recovery plan she designed was the reason he healed so fast.
She watched her daughter blow out the candles on the cake she'd baked from scratch.
He forwarded the finished project to the whole team a full day ahead of schedule.
She stood at the summit marker, having led the group the entire way up.
He told his old friend about the promotion, sitting a little straighter as he spoke.
She paid off the loan in full and filed the last statement away for good.
sad: She stared out the window the whole ride, barely noticing the stops go by.
He walked out of the building and sat in his car for a long time before starting the engine.
She pushed the food around her plate, saying little through the whole meal.
He watched the rain from the doorway, arms wrapped around himself, saying nothing.
She folded the paper twice and put it at the bottom of her bag.
He took one last look at the empty room and closed the door slowly behind him.
She sat alone on the bench long after the others had left the field.
He made just enough for one and ate standing at the counter.
She watched the plane taxi away from the window, then turned and walked back through the empty terminal.
He sat by the bed in silence, holding a hand that no longer squeezed back.
She blew out the candles alone and put the extra slice back in the fridge.
He read the rejection email twice before closing the laptop for the night.
She turned back halfway up the trail and walked down slower than she'd walked up.
His voice trailed off mid-sentence, and neither of them tried to fill the silence.
She read the number twice, set the envelope down, and didn't open the others.
desperate: He kept checking the clock and switching lanes, gripping the wheel tighter with every red light.
She rehearsed her answers under her breath outside the door, hands shaking as she reached for the handle.
He kept glancing at his phone under the table, willing it to ring with any answer at all.
They piled sandbags against the door as the water kept rising past the porch steps.
She refreshed the results page over and over, heart pounding each time it failed to load.
He called every number in his contacts trying to find anyone free to help before the truck arrived.
With seconds on the clock, she sprinted the length of the field, lungs burning, refusing to slow down.
He threw ingredients together with shaking hands, the guests already at the door and nothing ready.
She ran through the terminal, boarding pass crumpled in her fist, watching the gate numbers blur past.
He paced the waiting room, calling anyone who might know a specialist, phone pressed hard to his ear.
She scrambled to find a replacement cake an hour before guests arrived, calling every bakery still open.
He typed as fast as he could, glancing at the clock every few seconds as it ran out.
They scanned the darkening trail for any sign of the marker, flashlight beams sweeping faster and faster.
She dialed again and again, praying someone would finally pick up.
He moved money between three accounts, trying to cover the payment before the deadline hit.
angry: He slammed his palm on the wheel as the light turned red for the third time in a row.
She walked out and yanked her coat off the hook, muttering under her breath the whole way to the elevator.
He shoved his chair back from the table and left the room without finishing his plate.
She kicked the fallen branch out of the driveway, cursing the tree she'd asked someone to trim for months.
He crumpled the paper in his fist and threw it across the room.
She snapped at the movers for the third time about the box they'd dropped.
He kicked the water bottle across the sideline after the referee's call.
She dropped the pan into the sink harder than she needed to and turned off the stove without plating anything.
He argued loudly with the gate agent, jabbing a finger at the screen showing the delay.
She raised her voice at the front desk, demanding to know why no one had called them back.
He stormed out to the backyard after the argument over the cake, slamming the door behind him.
She fired off a sharp email to the whole team the moment she saw the missed deadline.
He threw his pack down on the trail after the map turned out to be wrong again.
Her voice rose sharply and she hung up before he could finish the sentence.
He tore open the envelope, read the charge, and immediately dialed the company, already raising his voice.

neutral_baseline_stories: He drove the usual route to work, stopping twice for traffic lights before parking in his regular spot.
She arrived ten minutes early, filled out the form at the front desk, and waited to be called in.
They set the table, served the pasta, and passed the bread basket around twice.
The forecast called for rain starting in the afternoon, with clearing skies expected by evening.
The results were posted online at nine in the morning as scheduled.
The moving truck arrived at eight, and the crew began loading boxes from the garage first.
The match started on time, and the first half ended with the ball mostly in midfield.
The recipe called for simmering the sauce for twenty minutes while the pasta cooked separately.
The flight was scheduled to board at gate 14, forty minutes before departure.
Visiting hours ran from two to six, and the room was on the third floor.
The invitations listed a start time of four o'clock at the community hall.
The report was due at five, and the file was saved to the shared drive that morning.
The trail was six miles round trip with about a thousand feet of elevation gain.
The call lasted about fifteen minutes, mostly covering scheduling for next week.
The statement listed the usual monthly charges along with one itemized service fee.

How do you convert kilometers to miles roughly?
What material are most US pennies made of today?
Can you name a constellation visible in the northern winter sky?
